paper_title: Recursive Environment Scaling for General Long-Horizon Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We study environment scaling as a way to increase agent-benchmark difficulty while holding core task objectives fixed. Our framework, Recursive Environment Scaling (RES), transforms existing benchmark environments while preserving their objectives and completion requirements. A proposer changes information access, resource relations, and execution dependencies; execution-grounded checks validate the resulting candidate, and accepted changes are inherited across rounds. This produces related environments for paired evaluation and training-trajectory collection. Experiments on 294 initial tasks from three benchmarks show lower task success for all six evaluation models, with decreases of 57.14--77.14 percentage points on Claw-Eval-Live. With equal trajectory counts and identical optimization settings, fine-tuning on RES trajectories outperforms original-trajectory SFT in all nine model--benchmark comparisons by 7.00--14.61 percentage points. Ablations identify recursive inheritance and dependency composition as important contributors to increased difficulty. Together, these results support environment scaling for both agent evaluation and training.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Language model agents increasingly perform tasks through extended interaction with digital environments. AgentBench (Liu et al., 2024) examines decisions across diverse environments, OSWorld (Xie et al., 2024) tests real computer use, and TheAgentCompany (Xu et al., 2025) evaluates workplace workflows. Across these settings, difficulty depends on how information is organized, resources are connected, and earlier actions constrain later ones. This makes the environment itself useful object of study when scaling agent evaluation. Recent work expands agent experience through task synthesis and environment construction. TaskCraft (Shi et al., 2025) scales the depth and breadth of tool-use tasks; LOGIGEN (Zeng et al., 2026) grounds task construction in executable policies and state verification. RST (Li et al., 2026b) recursively extends reference solutions and realigns instructions and verifiers with the resulting workflows. At the environment level, EnvScaler (Song et al., 2026) synthesizes tool-interaction sandboxes, and ScaleEnv (Tu et al., 2026) constructs interactive environments and verifiable tasks from scratch. RES transforms existing benchmark environments under fixed task objectives and completion requirements, enabling paired evaluation across descendants. WorkArena++ (Boisvert et al., 2024) composes multi-step knowledge-work tasks, while τ 2-Bench (Barres et al., 2025) couples agent and user actions through shared state. These settings highlight how dependencies shape task execution. Changing access paths and prerequisites can lengthen tasks workflow while preserving the information and operations needed for completion. This motivates our research question: How can we recursively scale executable environments while preserving core task objectives? We introduce Recursive Environment Scaling (RES) (Figure 1). proposer inspects validated parent environment and composes programmatic transformations of its resources and execution dependencies. Execution-grounded checks determine whether the candidate realizes the proposed changes and preserves task validity. Accepted children are inherited for subsequent construction, allowing later transformations to build on earlier structures. Target-agent evaluation measures difficulty separately from environment acceptance. The lineages support paired evaluation and training-trajectory collection. Figure 2 summarizes performance, interaction demand, and environment structure on Claw-Eval-Live. Across six models and three benchmarks, RES reduces task success in all 18 comparisons. On Claw-Eval-Live, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash falls from 82.86% to 5.71%. With equal-sized training sets, RES trajectories also improve all three Qwen3.5 Base models over original-trajectory SFT on every benchmark. Our contributions are threefold: 1. Environment Scaling. We study existing benchmark environments as scaling dimension, preserving core task objectives while transforming information access and execution dependencies. 2. RES Framework. We combine proposer-guided transformations, execution-grounded validation, and 2 Figure 3 Overview of RES. The proposer transforms accepted parent Ek. Execution-grounded checks validate the changes, task validity, and dependency feasibility, guiding revisions before accepting child. Accepted children become parents; target evaluation separately informs stopping. recursive inheritance to accumulate accepted changes along each task lineage. 3. Empirical Evidence. RES reduces task success across six models and improves SFT across three backbones; ablations assess inheritance and dependencies.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Evaluating agents in executable environments. SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2024) and Terminal-Bench (Merrill et al., 2026) cover repository and command-line tasks. WebArena (Zhou et al., 2024) and WebVoyager (He et al., 2024) evaluate website interaction, with BrowserGym (de Chezelles et al., 2025) providing shared interfaces. WorkArena (Drouin et al., 2024) studies enterprise workflows; τ -Bench (Yao et al., 2024) couples tool use with domain policies and final-state checks. AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024) spans applications, while Claw-Eval-Live (Li et al., 2026a) and Workspace-Bench (Tang et al., 2026) emphasize execution evidence and file dependencies. Task and trajectory construction. Mind2Web (Deng et al., 2023) collects human action sequences across websites. TaskCraft (Shi et al., 2025) expands task depth and breadth, while LOGIGEN (Zeng et al., 2026) grounds construction in executable policies and state verification. DIVE (Chen et al., 2026) uses executed tool traces, and CLI-Universe (Hua et al., 2026) grounds terminal tasks in technical material. RST (Li et al., 2026b) extends reference solutions recursively and realigns instructions and verifiers. RES keeps core task requirements fixed while transforming the environment. Environment construction and adaptation. SWE-Gym (Pan et al., 2025) packages tasks with runtimes and tests, and AgentGym (Xi et al., 2025) supports exploration and training across environments. EnvScaler (Song et al., 2026) synthesizes tool-interaction sandboxes; ScaleEnv (Tu et al., 2026) builds tools, dependency graphs, and verifiable tasks from scratch. Agent-World (Dong et al., 2026) combines environment discovery with training arena, and Gym-Anything (Aggarwal et al., 2026) configures real software for computer use. SPICE (Liu et al., 2025) grounds self-play in document corpus, while SPADE (Liu et al., 2026) trains an environment designer jointly with learner. RES recursively inherits accepted changes to existing benchmarks, supporting paired difficulty evaluation and training-trajectory collection.

sections.title: 3.1 Problem Formulation and Overview
sections.content: We represent task at recursion step by (Ck, Ek), where Ck specifies its objective, constraints, and completion conditions, and Ek contains the executable resources, states, operations, and interaction dependencies. RES fixes the core objective, underlying facts, and completion requirements; specification updates describe the access instructions needed after environmental changes. validated seed starts recursive environment lineage: (C0, E0) (C1, E1) (CK, EK). (1) The proposer composes transformation plan Πk for the accepted parent. Executing this plan produces candidate, (cid:101)Ek+1 = Apply(Ek, Πk), (2) which becomes the next parent only after validation (Section 3.3). Figure 3 illustrates the procedure. Public instructions describe revised access paths and prerequisites, allowing the agent to recover the information needed for the original required outputs.

sections.title: 3.2 Environment Transformation
sections.content: Planning and execution. The proposer conditions its plan on the task specification and current environment, selecting programmatic primitives, resource bindings, parameters, and their composition. Resource transformations change information access; relational transformations alter relationships among sources; operational transformations modify when actions become available. The plan binds transformations to concrete resources and orders their execution. Applying it produces the interfaces and state transitions that the target encounters (Equation 2). Benchmark-specific resource bindings and the transformation library are described in Appendices and D.1. Dependency composition. RES connects transformations so that one operation can consume information or state produced by another. Dependencies may combine several prerequisites before enabling an action or propagate state changes to later operations. Subsequent generations can extend these structures, adding interaction requirements while retaining valid solution path. For example, an evidence view may require link query and export preparation. later transformation can add index recovery before that view. The inherited procedure becomes part of longer execution path around the same objective, as the reconciliation case in Section 5.4 illustrates.

sections.title: 3.3 Validated Environment Construction
sections.content: Task preservation and validation. Acceptance checks task preservation, construction consistency, and public executability. The verifier checks the parent lineage and protected task requirements, then independently replays the declared transformations from the fixed parent. The rebuilt executable definition must match the submitted candidate. We write the validation decision as vk = (Ck+1, Ek, Πk, (cid:101)Ek+1; ξk), (3) where ξk denotes replay and execution evidence. In fresh session, the verifier follows public interfaces to resolve references, execute preparation steps, and reconstruct transformed resources. Recovered content is compared with source facts; missing records, invalid references, and unsatisfied prerequisites reject the candidate. These checks cover the transformed access paths while preserving the original completion requirements (Appendix A). Repair. Failed checks return diagnostics about unsatisfied requirements, construction mismatches, or invalid dependencies. The proposer revises the affected resource bindings, parameters, or operation sequence and resubmits the candidate. Repair changes the proposed child while preserving the accepted parent. Candidates still invalid at the repair limit are discarded, leaving that parent available for subsequent construction. sections.title: 3.4 Recursive Environment Scaling
sections.content: The validated child becomes the next parent, preserving its resources and dependencies. Later plans reuse existing access paths and attach prerequisites to inherited operations, so accepted changes accumulate along the lineage. We evaluate the original and last accepted environments, plus intermediate generations requested by the proposer, under the protocol in Appendix A. At measured nodes, three assessed failures with no measurement errors stop further descendants. Transformation planning and acceptance use the environment and validation evidence. Recursion ends at budget or stopping condition, with the last accepted snapshot retained as the scaled environment.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We test whether RES makes existing benchmarks more demanding across six evaluation models and improves training across three Qwen3.5 Base backbones.

sections.content: Benchmarks and models. Each task defines paired comparison between its original environment and the last environment accepted by RES. We evaluate DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 5, GLM-5.2, Qwen3.8-Max, and Kimi K3 on both versions. sections.title: 4.2 Scaling Benchmark Difficulty
sections.content: Environment scaling reduces task success across models. Table 1 shows lower success in all 18 model benchmark comparisons. On Claw-Eval-Live, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash drops from 82.86% to 5.71%, while Claude Opus 5 drops from 86.67% to 28.57%. The reduction spans 12.0019.00 percentage points on WorkspaceBench-Lite and 41.5747.19 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. Under the same single-attempt evaluation budget, the scaled environments are consistently harder across the model suite. Requirement completion also declines. Every model obtains lower Claw native score and Workspace RPR after scaling. For GPT-5.6 Sol, Claw native score falls from 91.24 to 35.44; Workspace RPR reductions range from 5.52 to 10.81 points across the model suite. Agents therefore satisfy fewer underlying requirements as well as complete fewer tasks. Section 5.2 examines how this decline develops with recursive depth and increased interaction demand.

sections.title: 5.1 Ablation Studies
sections.content: We examine dependency composition, recursive inheritance, depth, and library breadth on Claw-Eval-Live  (Table 3)  . DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash makes one attempt per environment with 50-turn limit and success threshold 0.80. Component comparisons share 15 tasks; depth analysis uses 105 frozen lineages. Protocols and per-task results appear in Appendices and D.2. Dependency composition increases difficulty. Removing cross-operator references and preparation prerequisites from saved RES environments, while retaining task facts and atomic transformation histories, raises pass@1 from 0.0% to 100.0% and mean native score from 7.73 to 92.93. Mean turns fall from 50.0 to 19.1, linking the removed prerequisites to both completion and interaction cost. Recursive inheritance accumulates enhancement. For planned depth di, we compare recursive construction with di independent enhancements of the original environment, evaluating the predeclared last construction. Both use the same nominal proposer-call limit per enhancement. The recursive control yields 6.7% pass@1 versus 93.3% independently, with scores of 14.40 versus 88.73 and approximately 2.5 times the mean target-token expenditure. Inheriting earlier changes therefore produces harder environments under matched construction opportunities. Additional depth strengthens enhancement. Applying depth caps to the same 105 lineages, with early-stopped finals retained, reduces pass@1 from 82.9% at E0 to 60.0% after one round, 17.1% at depth two, and 4.8% at depth ten. Mean native score falls from 87.84 to 13.37. These retained-environment measurements show gains beyond one round; Appendix C.3 reports all caps and distinguishes them from historical averages. 7 Figure 4 Historical performance and interaction demand on Claw-Eval-Live. Restricting transformations to Basic subset of six mechanisms, with recursion and planned depths unchanged, raises pass@1 from 6.7% to 80.0% and native score from 14.40 to 85.73 relative to the shared regenerated control. The full library gives the proposer more effective ways to compose environmental requirements.

sections.title: 5.2 Cumulative Effects of Recursive Environment Scaling
sections.content: We fix DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and 50-turn budget per attempt. Figure 4 reports historical means from E0 through each depth budget over the same 105 tasks, retaining final environments for early-stopped chains (Appendix C). Success and partial completion decline together. From budget zero to ten, historical mean success falls from 82.86% to 18.18%, and mean native score from 0.878 to 0.260. The two measures show decline in both task success and partial completion under this benchmark-level aggregation. Interaction demand increases. Under the same aggregation, mean turns rise from 3.55 to 43.22 and tool calls from 8.05 to 206.02; the turn-limit rate reaches 75.06%. These measurements include successful and unsuccessful trajectories. Depth and endpoint evaluations use separate batches; Appendix reports the retained-state results and depth counts.

sections.title: 5.3 Environment Scaling Efficiency and Cost
sections.content: On Claw-Eval-Live, RES produces 289 accepted children from 105 seeds. Of these, 92.0% require at most two outer proposer executions; mean costs are 1.45 executions, 89.2k tokens, and 112.6 seconds per child. Figure 5 shows fewer outer executions but greater token use at later stages, so execution counts alone do not capture scaling cost. Adaptive stopping also changes which tasks reach later stages. Costs cover executions associated with accepted children, excluding unsuccessful branches, target solving, and grading. An outer execution may contain multiple model requests and tool calls; time sums execution durations. Full definitions and distributions appear in Appendix A. 8 Figure 5 Proposer cost across recursive stages. Bars and lines show the same per-child means on Claw-Eval-Live. Depths 14 contain 105, 94, 57, and 18 children; dark bars pool 15 children from five seeds at depths 510. Time sums proposer execution durations. Figure 6 Recursive scaling of financial reconciliation task. Access and recovery dependencies accumulate while the reconciliation objective is preserved. The diagram shows E0E2; endpoint evaluation uses final E3.

sections.title: 5.4 Case Study: Three-Source Financial Reconciliation
sections.content: Task A01 in Claw-Eval-Live requires matching CRM, bank, and invoice records, identifying discrepancies, and producing reconciliation report. In E0, the agent can read three CSV files directly. E1 introduces link queries and export preparation before linked view can be accessed. E2 inherits these steps and adds archive, schema, and index-recovery dependencies (Figure 6); final E3 adds encoding constraints. Evidence-access requirements accumulate around the preserved core reconciliation objective. In the independent paired evaluation, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash makes 171 tool calls in the scaled environment, compared with three in the original environment, while its native score falls from 0.98 to zero. The trajectory includes reference queries, export preparation, and index rebuilding, with one batched query covering 37 references. The agent reaches the 50-turn limit while still acquiring evidence and does not complete the reconciliation report. The added work is concentrated before reconciliation: the original three reads expose the needed records directly, whereas the scaled environment requires the agent to resolve inherited access 9 and recovery dependencies. This case links the observed increase in interaction demand to the operations introduced along the lineage. Validation and target evaluation provide complementary evidence in this example. Restoration checks verify that the required records remain recoverable through public operations. The rollout then measures whether the agent can complete the original report within its budget. Its failure during evidence acquisition connects the lower score to the added access procedure. The objective and required deliverable stay fixed throughout this comparison.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: RES makes existing executable environments controllable dimension of agent evaluation and training. Under preserved core task objectives, recursively inherited transformations reduce task completion across three benchmarks and six models, while the resulting training trajectories improve all three Qwen3.5 Base models over original-trajectory SFT. Component ablations and trajectory analysis connect these observations to inherited dependencies and increased interaction demand. These results support environment scaling as practical way to extend existing benchmarks and collect training trajectories that improve agent performance.

sections.title: A Evaluation and Environment Scaling
sections.content: Evaluation protocol. We separate the target evaluations used to stop environment scaling from the independent evaluations used to report benchmark performance. During scaling, three attempts test complete task fulfilment. After scaling, we freeze the environments and run one attempt per task. On Claw-Eval-Live, independent evaluation counts native scores of at least 0.80 as successful. Table A1 summarizes the scaling, depth-reevaluation, and model-comparison settings. Table A1 Protocols for environment scaling and independent evaluation on Claw-Eval-Live. Scaling-stage attempts determine when to stop recursion; depth reevaluation measures changes over saved lineages; the paired model comparison evaluates original and RES-scaled environments. model turn is one target-model response, potentially containing multiple tool calls. Stopping uses complete fulfilment; independent success uses native-score threshold of 0.80. Environment scaling Depth reevaluation Model comparison Attempts per environment 3 at evaluated nodes Model-turn limit Success criterion Target Task cohort 60 Complete task fulfilment DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 105 seeds Primary use Stopping decisions 1 50 Native score 0.80 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 105 seeds / 394 environments Recursive trends 1 50 Native score 0.80 Six evaluation models 105 matched seeds per model Original vs. RES Scaling configuration. GPT-5.6 Sol with high reasoning effort proposes transformations. Each lineage has maximum depth of 10 and budget of eight outer proposer executions per parent, including repairs and retries. We process 32 seeds concurrently; the three target attempts within each seed run sequentially. Every lineage includes evaluation of its original and last accepted environments, with intermediate evaluations requested by the proposer. Target outcomes determine stopping; the validation procedure in Section 3.3 determines whether child is accepted. Target configuration. Across all three benchmarks, target attempts have 60-turn limit during scaling and 50-turn limit during independent evaluation, with at most 16,384 output tokens per response. Timeouts follow the task-specific Claw configuration: 180, 240, 300, 420, or 600 seconds, held fixed within each original/scaled pair. All six evaluation models use high reasoning effort. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash uses thinking with high effort throughout scaling, depth reevaluation, and the frozen endpoint comparison. Workspace and terminal evaluation. Workspace-Bench-Lite contains 100 tasks and Terminal-Bench 2.1 contains 89. The latter uses the official 2.1 revision, which fixes 28 tasks from the 2.0 release.1 Both follow the scaling and target configurations above. Paired environments use the same model settings, tool permissions, and scoring protocol. Workspace TCR@80 counts tasks that pass at least 80% of their rubric items; RPR pools passed items across tasks. Terminal-Bench uses its executable verifiers binary result. Success rates weight tasks equally. Validation and stopping. Claw validation checks lineage and protected-contract hashes, replays the declared operators from the frozen parent, and compares the rebuilt files with the candidate. The original goal, facts, and grader remain fixed. Public traversal reconstructs files and service records, rejecting content loss or duplication, invalid references, nonterminating preparation, and original-file bypasses. The record stores replay hashes and execution traces. Stopping requires three assessed failures with no measurement errors. 1Terminal-Bench 2.1 release notes. 13 Table A2 Proposer construction cost per accepted Claw-Eval-Live child. Mean, median, and 90th-percentile (P90) costs cover all 289 children constructed by GPT-5.6 Sol with high reasoning effort. Each childs costs aggregate its outer executions and retries. Tokens include input and output; time sums execution durations. Target solving and grading are excluded. Quantity Outer proposer executions Input + output tokens (k) Summed execution time (s) Mean 1.45 89.19 112.61 Median 1.00 65.27 93. P90 2.00 179.82 184.00 Workspace and terminal adapters. Workspace transformations act on files, structured records, and workflow dependencies. The adapter binds derived views to source hashes and checks restored files or projected records against frozen inputs; Office and PDF resources are inspected with native readers. Reported TCR@80 and RPR use the frozen benchmark rubric. Terminal transformations act on container files, build configurations, database states, and service inputs. Frozen parent state and declared resource bindings identify the inputs to each child. Materialized artifacts undergo native readback and execution checks, and task scoring uses the executable verifier. Private tests and reference solutions remain on the evaluator side. Environment validity and manual review. Three researchers reviewed 20 matched original/scaled pairs from each benchmark: 60 task lineages and 120 endpoint environments in total. They checked core objectives, required information, scoring conditions, answer leakage, and scoring bypasses, alongside programmatic checks of executability and taskevaluation consistency. None of these issues was found in the reviewed samples. Construction cost. The 289 accepted children account for 420 outer executions, 25.78M input and output tokens, and 9.04 hours of summed proposer execution time. We first add the executions associated with each child, including retries, then compute the statistics in Table A2. Of these children, 193 require one execution and 73 require two, accounting for 92.0% together. Input totals include cached tokens; reasoning tokens are included once in the reported totals. Time measures summed execution durations under concurrent processing. These costs cover accepted-child construction and exclude branches producing no child, target solving, grading, and orchestration overhead.

sections.title: B Training Data and Optimization
sections.content: Training conditions. At each model scale, SFT w/o RES and SFT w/ RES start independently from the same Base checkpoint and use 8,428 trajectories with identical optimization settings (Table A3). The original trajectories are drawn from ClawGym and generated by DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. For SFT w/ RES, RES is applied to this training task pool and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash collects new trajectories in the scaled environments, using the same selection and supervision rules. Evaluation uses the original environments of the 294 benchmark tasks in Table 2. Original-trajectory data. We select 8,428 distinct tasks from the released ClawGym task and trajectory collections, retaining one structurally complete rollout per task.2 We deduplicate records across release formats and require traceable task association, complete messages, matched tool calls and returns, and released native score of at least 0.8. Filtering uses the released scores without replaying the trajectories. The selected data contain 3,381 full-score and 5,047 partial-score trajectories, each no longer than 49,152 tokens. This original-trajectory set contains 190.52M input tokens and 39.74M supervised target tokens; its median sequence length is 20,195 tokens. Supervision. Training preserves the available reasoning, tool calls, tool outputs, and final responses. Loss applies to assistant reasoning, responses, and unmasked tool calls. Calls with missing parameters or unverified semantics remain in context but are excluded from the loss; the original-trajectory set contains 78 such calls from 54 tasks. custom ms-swift template preserves these token-level supervision labels. Optimization. We run one epoch of full-parameter SFT in BF16 on four H800 GPUs. per-device batch of one with four accumulation steps gives global batch of 16, with 12 examples in the last of 527 updates. We evaluate the final checkpoint; training uses no held-out validation split. Table A3 lists the hyperparameters. The software stack consists of ms-swift 4.6.0.dev0, PyTorch 2.11.0, Transformers 5.16.1, and DeepSpeed 0.19.6. Evaluation-overlap checks. We screened the training tasks against all three evaluation benchmarks and found no matches under the checks performed: 105 Claw-Eval-Live, 100 English Workspace-Bench-Lite, and 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks. The Claw and Workspace records compare task identifiers, task text, input-content hashes, and lexical similarity. These checks address the recorded task and input representations.

Evaluation and generation budgets. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash evaluates each component condition with thinking and high reasoning effort, 50-turn limit, and at most 16,384 output tokens per response. It also supplies the native grade; weighted score of at least 0.80 counts as pass. GPT-5.6 Sol proposes transformations with high reasoning effort and nominal budget of eight outer Codex executions per parent, covering queries, construction, repairs, and retries. We record proposer tokens without imposing token cap, so matching construction opportunities does not imply equal realized token cost. The depth analysis is separate batch of 394 task-environment evaluations with reported outcomes.
